strengths: Comprehensive empirical ablations (Tables 1–5) systematically investigate CLIP design choices for 3D medical imaging, providing valuable practical guidance
Identifies and addresses domain-specific challenges: long medical reports vs. short prompts (quantified 10-point gap), field-of-view requirements, and long token sequences (14k tokens)
Strong results on global tasks: +2 AUPRC/+1.5 AUROC classification probing improvement, +17 RadBERT MacroF1 in report generation, competitive zero-shot classification (77.8% AUROC native)
Holistic evaluation across diverse tasks (retrieval, classification, report generation, segmentation) fairly demonstrates strengths and limitations
Practical contributions: structured report preprocessing pipeline using LLM categorization, sentence shuffling regularization, and reproducible augmentation strategies
Excellent reproducibility: detailed appendices with preprocessing, hyperparameters, metrics, and thorough evaluation protocols
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging prompt brittleness, poor segmentation scaling, and methodological trade-offs rather than overstating results
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: combines existing components (CLIP, CapPa RRG, MAE) without introducing new techniques; primarily domain engineering rather than algorithmic innovation

Multi-objective incoherence: RRG improves retrieval but decreases classification probing (56.58 vs. 58.02 AUPRC) and zero-shot performance (75.27 vs. 78.33 AUROC); MAE barely improves segmentation despite being proposed for dense tasks, while standalone MAE outperforms by 4–6 Dice points

Severe segmentation underperformance: COLIPRI models marginally exceed from-scratch baseline on LiTS/Lung/KiTS23; contradicts stated goal of improving dense tasks that represent 'majority of challenges in medical imaging'
Zero-shot classification brittleness: 7–10 AUROC point gap between native and short prompts indicates poor semantic robustness; acknowledged but unresolved, problematic for clinical deployment
Narrow experimental scope: single region (chest CT) and modality; no validation on other anatomies or modalities; claims of 'comprehensive' pre-training overstated
Report generation ground truth issues: absolute performance low (RadBERT F1 ~40%, RadFact(+) ~20%); clinical significance unclear; only Findings used (Impression omitted); uses basic LLaVA framework

Methodological mismatches undermine conclusions: pre-training uses -1/+1 Hounsfield normalization while segmentation uses CT normalization (acknowledged as suboptimal); 2mm vs. 1mm spacing mismatch; frozen encoder during report generation limits adaptation
Hyperparameter search concerns: star sweep may be incomplete; design choices (removing APE, specific probabilities) justified by small improvements potentially within noise; no sensitivity analysis
Inconsistent baselines: CT-CLIP underperforms original paper; uses flexible probing (5 aggregations × 4 learning rates) inflating all methods' performance, reducing fair comparison
Reproducibility gaps: GPT-4o version-dependent preprocessing; no mention of releasing checkpoints; implementation details of loss interaction unclear

Missing ablations: no evaluation of advanced MIM methods (iBOT, DINOv2, DINOv3) in 3D; unclear why MAE outperforms yet COLIPRI-CRM is preferred; no cross-anatomy transfer validation; no error analysis or qualitative failure cases

strengths: Addresses practical limitation: identifies and mitigates real challenges in 3D medical imaging (data scarcity, long reports, FOV requirements) with domain-informed solutions
Extensive ablation studies systematically investigate design choices (Tables 1-5), providing useful insights for practitioners on report length, patch sizes, batch sizes, and augmentations
Holistic evaluation across diverse downstream tasks (retrieval, classification probing, zero-shot classification, report generation, segmentation) with honest acknowledgment of limitations
Strong empirical results on global tasks: classification probing exceeds baselines by 1.5-2 AUROC points; report generation shows +17 RadBERT MacroF1 improvement
Transparent discussion of brittleness (zero-shot prompting sensitivity), weak segmentation performance, and preprocessing mismatches for downstream tasks
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily engineering/application of existing methods (CLIP, CapPa [42], MAE [13], vision-language+vision-only [24,26]); no fundamental algorithmic contributions

Contradictory core results undermine main claims: combined objectives (COLIPRI-CRM) underperform base CLIP (COLIPRI-C) on classification (56.96 vs 58.02 AUPRC) and zero-shot (83.77 vs 84.23 AUROC); MAE substantially outperforms all COLIPRI variants on segmentation (80.75 vs 76.93 DSC on LiTS), negating the 'comprehensive' framing

Severe brittleness of zero-shot classification: 7-10 AUROC point collapse from native (77.80) to short prompts (70.18) on CT-RATE; fundamental issue not solved, only acknowledged, limiting real-world deployment

Significant generalization gap: 11 AUROC point drop from CT-RATE to RAD-ChestCT in zero-shot classification; data preprocessing mismatch (normalization and spacing differences between pre-training and segmentation evaluation) explicitly undermines downstream performance

Baseline comparison issues: CT-CLIP reports much lower performance (61.21 AUROC) than original paper (75.1%) with acknowledged 'potential configuration issue'; Merlin trained on abdominal CTs (domain mismatch); mixed evaluation protocols limit fairness of comparisons

Report generation remains clinically unusable: absolute F1 scores very low (~40 MacroF1, ~20 F1+ in Table 9); improvement over baselines is relative only; confound from LLaVA framework makes it unclear whether gains are from encoder or LLM

Lack of statistical rigor: classification metrics lack error bars or significance testing; differences may not be statistically significant (84.15 vs 82.62 AUROC); only report generation includes confidence intervals

Ad-hoc methodological choices poorly justified: MAE included only in last 25% of training (no principled justification); LLM report shortening uses proprietary GPT-4o (not reproducible); field of view analysis (Table 2) explains results post-hoc rather than predicting them

Overclaimed scope: trained on chest CT only; 'comprehensive' claim contradicted by inability to achieve good dense task performance; limited modality and anatomical diversity undermines generalization claims

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: systematic study of vision-language pre-training for 3D medical imaging with thorough investigation of domain-specific design choices

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple tasks (retrieval, classification, report generation, segmentation) with strong clinical metrics showing +17 point MacroF1 improvement on report generation
Systematic and extensive ablation studies that provide practical design guidance for 3D medical imaging (report augmentation, field-of-view tradeoffs, token aggregation strategies)
Thorough documentation of methodology enabling reproducibility with extensive implementation details and prompts provided
Well-motivated solutions to domain challenges, particularly sentence shuffling and shortening to address distribution shift between long training reports and short zero-shot prompts
Strong performance on global tasks (classification probing, zero-shot classification, report generation) with competitive or state-of-the-art results
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily adapts existing methods (CLIP, CapPa, MAE) to 3D medical domain rather than introducing new algorithms or concepts

Weak segmentation results contradict stated goals: COLIPRI shows minimal improvement over scratch (76.93 vs 74.51 DSC on LiTS) and lags far behind MAE baseline (80.75 DSC), suggesting objectives don't synergize as intended for dense tasks

Heavy reliance on GPT-4 for report preprocessing (translation, structuring, shortening) makes reproducibility difficult and raises questions about whether improvements come from the method or GPT-based data curation

Significant prompt sensitivity in zero-shot classification (10-point AUROC gap between native/short prompts) reveals limited robustness; acknowledged but not addressed despite being critical for deployment

Conflicting results undermine complementarity claims: RRG objective designed for report generation decreases classification performance; COLIPRI-CRM underperforms COLIPRI-C on some tasks, with limited mechanistic understanding
Sophisticated classification probing setup (5 aggregation schemes × 4 learning rates) complicates direct comparison with simpler baselines and may inflate apparent gains over CT-CLIP

Generalization concerns: method trained only on chest CT (~78k pairs, vastly smaller than general CLIP), with 11-point AUROC degradation on external dataset suggesting overfitting; unclear transfer to other body regions or modalities

Possible data leakage during development: CT-RATE validation set used for hyperparameter selection before final evaluation, with observable performance drop on external dataset suggesting dataset-specific overfitting

Missing mechanistic analysis: insufficient investigation of why multi-objective training sometimes hurts performance or why MAE provides minimal segmentation benefit despite being strong standalone baseline

strengths: Well-motivated domain-specific problem addressing real challenges in 3D medical imaging (data scarcity, computational constraints, train-test mismatch)
Novel Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL) that elegantly handles diagnostic polarity distinction without requiring spatial grounding
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple downstream tasks (classification, zero-shot, retrieval, segmentation, report generation) with extensive ablations
Strong empirical results: +3.5 AUROC on classification, +2.0 on zero-shot over strong baselines, +23 RadBERT F1 on report generation
Systematic staged development (COLIPRI-C/CR/CM/CRM) clearly demonstrating contribution of each component
Thoughtful domain-specific engineering (sentence shuffling, LLM-based report structuring, multi-resolution exposure)
High reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and promised code/weights release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines established techniques (CLIP, MAE, transformer decoding); OSL is incremental (template negation + binary CE)
RRG objective underperforms expectations—contributes minimally to global tasks while adding computational overhead; inclusion not well justified

Clinical utility undemonstrated: absolute accuracies low (RadBERT F1 ~45%, RadFact F1 ~22%); work claims clinical applicability yet lacks radiologist evaluation and remains below clinical practice thresholds
Segmentation results disappoint on dense tasks: Transformer-based Primus-M consistently underperforms CNN baseline ResEnc-L; pre-training gains do not close architecture gap, limiting applicability

Classification probe methodology raises comparability concerns: multi-probe grid search with non-linear attention pooling differs fundamentally from fixed linear probing baselines; acknowledged superiority over baselines' setups makes direct comparison problematic
Substantial 10+ AUROC gap between classification probe (86%) and zero-shot classification (80%) contradicts main alignment claim
Limited domain scope: exclusively chest CT; generalization untested; segmentation evaluation only on in-distribution anatomies
Inconsistent experimental choices: segmentation uses different normalization than pre-training; acknowledged as suboptimal yet results reported without correction
GPT-4o dependency for report preprocessing and evaluation creates non-reproducible components; no ablation on whether LLM-based restructuring is necessary
OSL design lacks justification: softmax over 2 scores equivalent to sigmoid, template-based negation simplistic, loss weight and design choices not ablated
MAE pre-training adds complexity: requires separate initialization; Table D.5 shows 3–6 DSC point drops without it; unclear if justified versus simpler alternatives
Computational costs not discussed: training time, VRAM, inference latency omitted; practical deployment feasibility unclear
Report generation evaluation incomplete: only Findings section evaluated; Impression omitted to 'reduce redundancy' yet clinical practice requires both
Short vs. native zero-shot gap (6–8 AUROC) suggests brittleness to prompt formulation, indicating alignment not robustly learned

strengths: Comprehensive multi-task evaluation demonstrating versatility of learned representations across classification, retrieval, report generation, and segmentation
Extensive ablation studies with systematic investigation of design choices (FOV, patch size, aggregation, text augmentations)
Thoughtful approach to data efficiency by combining paired and unpaired datasets to address limited availability of medical imaging data
Strong empirical results on clinical metrics for report generation (23-point improvement in RadBERT MacroF1)
Detailed documentation and reproducibility commitment with promised model weights and code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core approach is direct CLIP application to 3D; RRG adapted from CapPa; MAE from existing work; only OSL is novel but represents an incremental contribution (contrastive loss over negated sentence pairs)

Inconsistent objective contributions: RRG objective produces only slight improvements and fails to improve the RRG task itself; COLIPRI-C/CR sometimes underperform COLIPRI-CM, suggesting RRG adds noise rather than signal; MAE is primary driver of improvements

Problematic experimental setup: Multi-probe linear probing setup (5 aggregation schemes × 4 learning rates, selected on validation) is significantly more flexible than standard approaches, making comparisons with other methods biased and unfair; acknowledged but unaddressed

Severely limited clinical applicability: Authors explicitly acknowledge performance is 'below thresholds typically expected in clinical practice'; absolute F1 scores remain very low (RadBERT ~45%, RadFact-CT(+) ~22%); 6.2-point gap between probing and zero-shot AUROC indicates poor alignment

Heavy LLM preprocessing dependency: Report structuring, shortening, and classification all use GPT-4o, making results non-reproducible and introducing confounds; unclear how much improvement stems from preprocessing vs. novel methods; preprocessing is orthogonal to core contributions

Technical contradictions: Paper argues large FOV is necessary for radiologist-centric understanding but empirically shows smaller inputs work better; uses 160×160×160 due to VRAM constraints despite claiming large FOV is required

Segmentation underperformance: Transformer architecture significantly lags CNN baselines (ResEnc-L); on Lung and HVS datasets, extended fine-tuning (250k steps) decreases performance—unusual and concerning; preprocessing mismatch between pre-training and evaluation normalizations

Limited scope and generalization concerns: Evaluation restricted to chest CT only; single-source dataset (CT-RATE from one hospital) without multi-site validation; domain bias not addressed; generalization to other body parts/modalities unknown
Semantic validation missing: OSL uses simplistic negation template ('No {sentence}') without analysis of negation quality or semantic soundness; no ablation on negation strategies or failure cases

Inconsistent statistical claims: Overlapping confidence intervals with baselines on key metrics (e.g., Table 1 AUPRC values); bootstrap samples may be insufficient (100-500); no significance testing beyond CIs

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies genuine challenges in 3D medical VLMs (limited paired data ~78k vs 400M for CLIP, computational constraints from high dimensionality, train-test mismatch between verbose reports and short zero-shot queries)

Novel Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL): Domain-aware solution that directly addresses linguistic mismatch through contrastive learning on positive/negative sentence pairs; shows 4pp AUROC improvement for short-form zero-shot classification

Comprehensive experimental validation: 6 downstream tasks, multiple datasets (CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, segmentation benchmarks), extensive ablations isolating each component's contribution, confidence intervals and bootstrap sampling (100-500 samples)

Strong empirical results: 6pp AUROC improvement in classification probing (86.12), 7pp in zero-shot (79.81), 23-point RadBERT MacroF1 improvement in report generation, 12× improvement in retrieval (R@5: 35.1% vs 2.9% CT-CLIP)

Thoughtful engineering: LLM-based report preprocessing addressing distribution shift, sentence augmentations motivated by linguistic analysis, alternating batch training to prevent objective interference, careful handling of class imbalance
Reproducibility: Model weights, inference code, and extensive methodological details (31-page appendix) will be released; enables community reproduction
Clear presentation: Well-structured with strong motivation, systematic methodology, effective visualizations (Figure 1 PCA), comprehensive ablations clearly presented
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: CLIP, MAE, and report generation are established techniques; OSL is straightforward application of contrastive learning with negations; core contribution is engineering existing methods rather than novel ideas

Clinical utility insufficient: Report generation F1 scores (~45% RadBERT MacroF1, ~22% RadFact-CT(+)) remain well below clinical deployment thresholds; authors acknowledge this gap but it limits real-world impact

Inconsistent individual objective contributions: RRG provides minimal benefit and sometimes degrades performance (e.g., retrieval R@5: 33.25 for CR vs 27.74 for C); segmentation gains are marginal (Lung: 67.56 vs 67.46 MAE); multimodal supervision doesn't consistently help dense tasks

Substantial alignment gap: 4.6pp AUROC gap between classification probes (86.12) and zero-shot (81.53) suggests embeddings not well-aligned for zero-shot; paper acknowledges but doesn't resolve this fundamental issue

Narrow scope and generalization concerns: All experiments on chest/abdominal CT; generalization to other anatomies or modalities unexplored; text encoder (CXR-BERT) pre-trained on X-rays may not transfer; raises questions about broader applicability

Non-standard evaluation methodology: Multi-probe classification scheme (5 pooling methods × 4 learning rates with validation set selection) conflates encoder quality with probe design and complicates baseline comparison; some baseline discrepancies (CT-CLIP: 75.1 reported vs 61.21 measured) raise reproducibility concerns

Reliance on GPT-4 for critical preprocessing: Report structuring, shortening, categorization depend on GPT-4 (v2024-08-06); if GPT-4 changes, results may not replicate; no robustness analysis for LLM errors in preprocessing

Preprocessing mismatch: Pre-training uses [-1000, 1000]→[-1, 1] normalization while segmentation uses nnU-Net CTNormalization; authors acknowledge this is 'not optimal' but proceed anyway, undermining segmentation comparisons
Hyperparameter tuning bias: Extensive star sweeps on CT-RATE validation set raises overfitting risk; no cross-dataset hyperparameter validation mentioned

Limited error analysis: No failure case discussion; PCA visualization is qualitative; lack of mechanistic analysis of learned representations; high variance in abnormality-wise results (Figure D.1) lacks interpretation
